extracted.intended_audience: trial judges and patent litigators (and juries)
extracted.subtask_description: Model jury instructions for patent trials covering invalidity defenses (anticipation, prior patents/applications, obviousness, enablement, written description) and damages (date, types, lost profits, reasonable royalty). Designed to be adapted by courts to instruct juries and to guide litigators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior invention (pre-AIA §102(g))
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim is invalid if the invention defined in that claim was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee invented it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence that (1) before the patentee invented his invention, the third party reduced to practice a product or method that included all of the features of the claim, or (2) the third party was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence in later reducing the invention to practice. The prior invention must be sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would have recognized it would work for its intended purpose. Practice Note: This defense may be negated if the invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed. Where priority of invention is a jury issue, further instructions about conception, reduction to practice, and diligence are required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abandonment, suppression, or concealment exception
rubrics_metrics.description: If the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed, it does not anticipate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may find abandonment, suppression, or concealment only if clear and convincing evidence shows (1) active concealment from the public, or (2) unreasonable delay in making the invention publicly known. Generally not abandoned/suppressed/ concealed if invention was made public, sold, offered for sale, or otherwise used commercially. A period of delay does not alone constitute abandonment if reasonable efforts were made to bring the invention to market. If this issue is asserted and supported, give additional instructions to the jury defining those terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent (pre-AIA §102(a),(b))
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the invention defined in the claim was disclosed in a patent in the United States or a foreign country before the relevant pre-AIA Cutoff Date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is a factual issue about the date of invention or priority date, instruct the jury on how to determine the date of invention; otherwise instruct as to the Cutoff Date. Court should include the invention date when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior patent (AIA §102(a)(1)/(b)(1) — patents as prior art)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent claim is invalid if the claimed invention was disclosed in a patent in the U.S. or a foreign country before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues exist about whether the disclosure resulted from the inventor or was obtained from the inventor (derivation) or whether the inventor had previously disclosed the subject matter, instruct the jury as to exceptions under §102(b)(1) as needed. State the effective filing date of the claimed invention when applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier-filed patent application (pre-AIA §102(e))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a published U.S. or PCT patent application or U.S. patent filed by another person before the patentee invented the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If jury must resolve date of invention, instruct how to determine it; otherwise instruct as to the filing date. Use these instructions where filing date of application/patent is the relevant date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Earlier-filed patent application (AIA §§102(a)(2), (b)(2), (c), & (d))
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is invalid if the invention was described in a published patent application or patent that was effectively filed before the effective filing date of the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues exist about whether the disclosure was obtained directly or indirectly from the inventor, was previously publicly disclosed by the inventor or another who obtained it from the inventor, or was owned/subject to obligation of assignment to the same person, instruct the jury on exceptions under §§102(b)(2) and (c) as needed. State the effective filing date and the effective filing date of the reference (per §102(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness — general standard
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention is invalid as obvious if it would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art as of the Cutoff Date. Unlike anticipation, obviousness may be shown by one or more prior art items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using hindsight — do not use the patent as a roadmap for selecting/combining prior art. Defendant must prove obviousness by clear and convincing evidence. Obviousness is a mixed question of fact and law; consider roles of court and jury and potential waiver of JMOL on appeal. Perform separate analysis for each claim alleged obvious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors for obviousness — scope and content of the prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the scope and content of the prior art relied upon by the defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior art considered includes items received into evidence. A reference may be considered if it discloses information designed to solve any problem addressed by the patent or has obvious uses beyond its main purpose such that a person of ordinary skill would reasonably examine it. Jury must decide whether a specific reference is prior art by clear and convincing evidence. Practice Note: If the PTO lacked material facts and new evidence is presented, instruct jury to evaluate whether evidence is materially new and consider its effect on clear-and-convincing burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors for obviousness — differences between claimed invention and prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: Analyze relevant differences between the prior art and the claimed invention from the viewpoint of a person of ordinary skill as of the Cutoff Date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine impact of differences on obviousness of the claimed invention as a whole. Consider inferences and creative steps a person of ordinary skill would have used; predictable results from combining known elements support obviousness; unexpected/unpredictable results or teachings away support nonobviousness. A claim is not proven obvious merely because each element was independently known. Consider whether a reason existed at the time to combine elements and whether there would have been a reasonable expectation of success. Consider 'teaching away' and, if inherency is alleged, instruct on inherency tailored to the evidence — inherency requires the element be the natural result of the explicit disclosure, not mere probabilities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors for obviousness — level of ordinary skill
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine the level of ordinary skill in the field of the invention at the Cutoff Date as part of the obviousness analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Person of ordinary skill is presumed to know all reasonably relevant prior art and to have ordinary creativity and common sense. If parties agree on level, state it. If not, consider evidence including (1) level of education and experience of persons in the field (including inventors), (2) types of problems encountered and prior art solutions, and (3) sophistication of the technology and rapidity of innovation at the Cutoff Date.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham factors for obviousness — secondary considerations (objective indicia)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consider secondary considerations that may help determine whether the invention would have been obvious, as part of the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations include: commercial success due to merits of the invention (not advertising or non-claimed features); long-felt but unsolved need satisfied by the invention; others tried and failed; copying by others; unexpectedly superior results over closest prior art; praise or surprise from others in the field or defendant; acceptance of licenses because of the merits. No single consideration is dispositive; relevancy requires a nexus between the consideration and the invention and admissibility is for the Court to decide. Patentee bears burden to show nexus. Consider these only if properly supported by evidence and analyze alongside other factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement requirement (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must disclose sufficient information to enable a person of ordinary skill in the field as of the effective filing date to make and use the full scope of the claimed invention without undue experimentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enablement is a question of law for the Court; jury may be instructed on subsidiary fact issues only if specific factual disputes bearing on enablement are submitted. Defendant bears burden by clear and convincing evidence that the specification fails enablement. Patents are written for persons of ordinary skill and need not state information such a person would likely know. Factors (Wands) to consider for undue experimentation include: quantity of experimentation and whether it uses known techniques; amount of direction/guidance in the patent; presence/absence of working examples; nature of the invention; state of the prior art; relative skill of those in the art; predictability of the art; and breadth of the claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description requirement (§112)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent must contain a written description of the product or method claimed to ensure the applicant actually invented the claimed subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written-description is a question of fact (instruct jury only if specific claims are challenged and evidence supports it). Defendant bears burden by clear and convincing evidence. The specification must describe each limitation of a claim with clear, concise, and exact terms; view the claim as a whole. Exact words need not be used; specific examples are not required. The written-description requirement is satisfied if a person of ordinary skill would recognize from the specification that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter as of the effective filing date. Consider factors including nature and scope of claims; complexity, predictability, and maturity of the technology; existing knowledge in the field; and scope/content of prior art. Sufficiency is decided claim-by-claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for invalidity challenges
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant bears the burden of proving patent invalidity defenses by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This standard applies to challenges such as anticipation, obviousness, enablement, and written-description. Obviousness, inherency, and prior-art status must be shown by clear and convincing evidence. Practice Note: If PTO examination lacked material facts, new evidence may make it easier for challenger to meet clear-and-convincing burden; jury may be instructed to consider whether evidence is materially new.

rubrics_metrics.name: Damages — general rule and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: If the accused device or method infringes and the claims are not invalid, the jury must determine the type and amount of damages to compensate the plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plaintiff must prove each element of damages, including amount, by a preponderance of the evidence (more likely than not). Damages must be adequate to compensate the plaintiff and cannot be punitive or include interest as an addition. If all asserted claims are invalid or not infringed, do not consider damages. Reasonable royalty is the minimum recoverable amount if infringement proven.

rubrics_metrics.name: Date damages begin — marking and notice rules
rubrics_metrics.description: The start date for damages depends on agreement or proof of when the defendant was put on notice of the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate A: parties may stipulate the start date. Alternate B: if disputed, the start date is when plaintiff first notified defendant of its patent claim. Plaintiff can give notice by marking substantially all products that practice the patent with the patent number (including virtual marking with internet address) or by direct specific notice to the defendant. Marking by licensees who use the patented invention also counts if they mark substantially all products. If plaintiff did not provide effective public marking and did not directly notify defendant, damages are recoverable only after the lawsuit filing date, except when plaintiff and licensees never made/offered/sold patented products (e.g., only method claims asserted)—then damages may be recovered up to six years before filing even without notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of patent damages — lost profits and reasonable royalty
rubrics_metrics.description: Available damages include lost profits (the additional profits the patentee would have made 'but for' the infringement) and reasonable royalty (what a willing licensee/licensor would have agreed to just before infringement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lost profits may include profits on sales lost due to infringement and under some circumstances profits lost on related products or price erosion. Reasonable royalty is the floor of damages. Plaintiff must prove damages elements by preponderance. See statutory law and case authorities cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lost profits — 'but for' test
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove lost-profits damages the plaintiff must show that, more likely than not, but for the defendant’s infringement, the plaintiff would have made additional profits through the sale of all or a portion of the defendant’s allegedly infringing sales.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jurors must determine what buyers who purchased/practiced defendant's products would have done absent infringement. The profits relevant are those allegedly lost by the plaintiff, not the defendant’s profits. Case law supports the 'but for' framework. (Panduit factors and further guidance follow in the instructions.)
